L13: # Data Independence
L14: A program P is data independent with respect to a data type X iff it does not use any operations and predicates involving values of type X other than equality tests. It is also allowed to input, output and nondeterministically choose values of type X, as well as store them and copy them within its variables. When P is data independent with respect to X, it is parameterised by X. In other words, any concrete data type can be instantiated for X in P.
L15: Given a specification S and a program P which are data independent with respect to a data type X, our main results on data independence enable the problem of verifying whether S is satisfied by P for all instances of X to be reduced to verifying the satisfaction for a finite number of finite instances. The body of research by which such results are proved is a semantic study of data independence consisting of symbolic operational semantics, logical relations, and symmetry elimination.
L16: Most of our research on data independence so far has been in terms of the CSP formalism. The basic part of the work can be found in Section 15.2 of "The Theory and Practice" book by A. W. Roscoe (available electronically in our 【11†books†web.comlab.ox.ac.uk】 section) and, in more detail, in Lazic's 【12†thesis†web.comlab.ox.ac.uk】.
L17: There also are papers on the extension by arrays in the context of determinism checking, and on the extension by generalised predicate symbols (see the group's 【13†publications page†web.comlab.ox.ac.uk】).

L33: ## Radu Grigore ; Nikos Tzevelekos - History-Register Automata
L34: 
L35: lmcs:1630 - Logical Methods in Computer Science, March 29, 2016, Volume 12, Issue 1 - 【30†https://doi.org/10.2168/LMCS-12(1:7)2016†doi.org】
L36: 
L37: History-Register Automata Article
L38: 
L39: Authors: Radu Grigore ; Nikos Tzevelekos
L40: Programs with dynamic allocation are able to create and use an unbounded number of fresh resources, such as references, objects, files, etc. We propose History-Register Automata (HRA), a new automata-theoretic formalism for modelling such programs. HRAs extend the expressiveness of previous approaches and bring us to the limits of decidability for reachability checks.
L41: The distinctive feature of our machines is their use of unbounded memory sets (histories) where input symbols can be selectively stored and compared with symbols to follow. In addition, stored symbols can be consumed or deleted by reset. We show that the combination of consumption and reset capabilities renders the automata powerful enough to imitate counter machines, and yields closure under all regular operations apart from complementation.
L42: We moreover examine weaker notions of HRAs which strike different balances between expressiveness and effectiveness.

L2: # A Logic for Fresh Labelled Transition Systems
L3: 
L4: Mohamed H. Bandukara m.h.bandukara@qmul.ac.uk Queen Mary University of London, UK Nikos Tzevelekos nikos.tzevelekos@qmul.ac.uk Queen Mary University of London, UK
L5: ###### Abstract
L6: We introduce a Hennessy-Milner logic with recursion for Fresh Labelled Transition Systems (FLTSs). These are nominal labelled transition systems which keep track of the history, i.e. of data values seen so far, and can model fresh data generation. In particular, FLTSs generalise the computations of Fresh-Register Automata, which in turn can be seen as a “regular” class of history-tracking automata operating on infinite input alphabets.
L7: The logic we introduce is a modal mu-calculus equipped with infinite disjunctions over arbitrary and fresh data values respectively, while its recursion is parameterised on vectors of data values. It can express a variety of properties, such as the existence of an infinite path of distinct data values, the absence of paths where values are repeated, or the existence of a finite path where some taint property is violated.
L8: We study the model-checking problem and its complexity via a reduction to parity games and, using nominal sets techniques, provide an exponential upper bound for it.

L43: ## 1 Introduction
L44: Nominal Labelled Transition Systems (LTSs) can capture computational scenarios which require unbounded sets of data values [【14†5】]. In the most elementary case, data values are just names, that is, atomic identifiers that can only be compared for equality. Nominal LTSs can be used, for example, for modelling mobile processes [【15†38】] and computation with variables [【16†24】, 【17†21】], and for verifying XML query languages [【18†41】].
L45: A particularly popular class of nominal LTSs are the ones generated by computations of “regular” automata over infinite alphabets, such as register automata [【16†24】] and the (largely) equivalent nominal automata [【14†5】]. A register automaton is equipped with a finite set of states, and hence the nod to regularity, but also a finite set of registers where it can store data values and compare them with, and possibly update them with, data values from the input.
L46: This design allows register automata to capture languages over infinite alphabets even though their specification is finite.
L47: Fresh-Register Automata (FRAs) [【19†44】] expand on this design by having the option of allowing the automaton to accept a name just if it is globally fresh, that is, it has not appeared so far in the input. FRAs can be used to capture computational models that use names and name generation, e.g. (finitary) $\pi $-calculus processes [【19†44】, 【20†3】] and programs with mutable references or objects [【21†35】, 【22†32】].
L48: They have been applied to program verification and system modelling, leading to verification tools [【22†32】, 【23†20】] and model learning techniques [【24†6】, 【25†1】]. Verification of FRAs has mainly focussed on bisimulation equivalence [【19†44】, 【26†33】, 【27†34】]. In this work we are interested in furthering formal verification for nominal computation, with an interest on FRAs and more generally history-dependent computation, in the direction of modal logics.
L49: Hennessy-Milner Logic (HML) is a modal behavioural logic that captures branching-time properties of labelled transition systems. It was initially introduced in 1980 by Hennessy and Milner [【28†22】] as an alternative exposition of observational equivalence [【29†8】]. Observational equivalence has a focus on testing whether two systems can simulate each other in a step-by-step manner, whereas HML logic focuses on the expressiveness of a single system.
L50: In image-finite systems, two states are equivalent just if they satisfy the same HML formulas [【30†23】]. The extension of HML with recursion, called modal $\mu $-calculus, was introduced by Kozen [【31†29】]. Here, we study a nominal extension thereof, where modalities are allowed to include names and where quantifications over some/all names and some/all fresh names are catered for. More specifically, our contributions include:
L51:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L52: 
L53: We introduce the notion of fresh LTS (FLTS), which extends nominal LTS with history dependence.
L54: 
L55:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L56: 
L57: We introduce fresh HML with recursion, in short $\mu $FHML, which allows us to express recursive branching-time properties involving names and name-freshness.
L58: 
L59:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L60: We study the model-checking problem for $\mu $FHML formulas on FLTSs. This leads us to developing parity games for $\mu $FHML and, through a series of reductions and using nominal techniques, devising a decision procedure for them.
L61: 
L62:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L63: 
L64: We provide (exponential) upper bound calculations for $\mu $FHML parity games and $\mu $FHML model checking, in the latter case both on general FLTSs and on FRAs.
L65: Although FRAs are our main target model, there are several advantages in defining and utilising FLTSs here. FLTS is a more general formalism, encompassing more scenarios besides FRAs (e.g. $\pi $-calculus processes). Actions performed in an FLTS can be more general than those given in FRAs, and allow e.g. for several fresh names to be generated at once or extra mechanisms for manipulating names between transitions (permutations, duplications, etc.).
L66: Additionally, FLTSs offer high-level reasoning and abstract away name/register manipulations.
L67: ### Related work.
L68: HML for the $\pi $-calculus was first examined in [【32†31】]. For properties involving paths of unbounded length, it is natural to examine recursive extensions thereof such as the modal $\mu $-calculus and variants thereof [【29†8】]. The logic we introduced is based on the $\pi $-$\mu $-calculus of Dam [【33†12】] and is related to the recent work on nominal $\mu $-calculi of Klin and collaborators [【34†26】, 【35†27】, 【36†15】].
L69: The $\pi $-$\mu $-calculus [【33†12】] specifically targets $\pi $-calculus processes, but the syntax used for recursion is the same as ours. The study of a history-dependent nominal $\mu $-calculus in [【36†15】] is the work closest to ours. In a certain sense, our work continues that of loc cit. by operating on history-dependent LTSs (and FRAs) and accommodating a vectorial version of recursion.
L70: We show that this combination still yields a decidable model-checking problem, and also provide a more algorithmic view on model checking via parity games and produce complexity bounds.
L71: In the area of nominal techniques, the modal logics for nominal LTSs by Parrow et al. [【37†37】] can subsume our logic but do not allow for decidable model checking. Logics for variants of register automata have been widely studied, e.g. [【38†42】, 【39†14】, 【40†18】]. The main focus of those works is on decidability, e.g. by restricting the number of registers allowed. No such restrictions are imposed on our logic, which is undecidable for satisfiability but our focus is instead on model checking.
L72: There have also been a series of works on logics related to the $\pi $-calculus, e.g. [【41†36】, 【42†28】, 【43†4】]. Those works mainly study expressiveness and characterisation of variants of behavioural equivalence for $\pi $-calculus processes. Other related works, such as [【44†11】, 【45†7】], expand on the modal $\mu $-calculus and study model checking, and show it to be decidable for finitary $\pi $-calculus processes.
L73: ## 2 Nominal sets and fresh labelled transition systems (FLTSs)
L74: We start by briefly introducing the nominal sets framework, which will be the basis of much of this paper. Let us fix $𝔸$ to be a countably infinite set of names (or data values) upon which nominal sets are built. A permutation $\pi $ on $𝔸$ (i.e. a bijection $\pi :𝔸\to 𝔸$) is considered finite if $\mathrm{supp}(\pi )=\{a\in 𝔸\mid \pi (a)\ne a\}$ is finite.
L75: For example, the identity permutation $id$ is finite ($id(a)=a$ for all $a\in 𝔸$) and, for any $a,b\in 𝔸$, so is the permutation $(ab)$ given by: $(ab)(a)=b$, $(ab)(b)=a$, and $(ab)(x)=x$ for all $x\ne a,b$. We denote the set of all finite permutations in $𝔸$ as $\mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}$.
L76: Given sequences of distinct names $\overrightarrow{a},\overrightarrow{b}\in {𝔸}^{k}$, we write $(\overrightarrow{a}\mapsto \overrightarrow{b})$ for the finite permutation obtained by canonically extending the map $\{({a}_{i},{b}_{i})\mid 1\le i\le k\}$.
L77: ###### Definition 1 ([【46†19】, 【47†39】]).
L78: 
L79: A nominal set $𝒳$ is a set $X$ equipped with an action from $\mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}$, i.e. a function $\mathrm{\_}\cdot \mathrm{\_}:\mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}\times X\to X$ such that for all $x\in X$ and $\pi ,{\pi }^{\prime }\in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}$:
L80: 
L81:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L82: 
L83: $\pi \cdot ({\pi }^{\prime }\cdot x)=(\pi \circ {\pi }^{\prime })\cdot x,id\cdot x=x$.
L84: A set of names $N\subseteq 𝔸$ supports an element $x\in X$ if, for all $\pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}$, if $\pi $ fixes all elements of $N$ then $\pi \cdot x=x$. We stipulate that all elements of $X$ be finitely supported, i.e. for all $x\in X$ there is some finite $N\subseteq 𝔸$ that supports $x$. We write $\mathrm{supp}(x)$ for the support of $x$, i.e. the least set supporting $x$. We say that $a$ is fresh for $x$, and write $a\mathrm{\#}x$, if $a\notin \mathrm{supp}(x)$.
L85: By abuse of notation, we may identify $𝒳$ with its carrier set $X$. The action on a nominal set extends to products and subsets by $\pi \cdot (x,y)=(\pi \cdot x,\pi \cdot y)$ and, for any $S\subseteq 𝒳$, by $\pi \cdot S=\{\pi \cdot x\mid x\in S\}$. Additionally, if $𝒳,𝒴$ are nominal sets then so is $𝒳\times 𝒴$, and the set of subsets of $𝒳$ with finite support.
L86: Accordingly, given a relation $R\subseteq 𝒳\times 𝒴$ and $\pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}$, we have $\pi \cdot R=\{(\pi \cdot x,\pi \cdot y)\mid (x,y)\in R\}$. We call $R$ equivariant if $\mathrm{supp}(R)=\mathrm{\varnothing }$, i.e. for all $\pi $ and $(x,y)\in 𝒳\times 𝒴$, $(x,y)\in R\iff (\pi \cdot x,\pi \cdot y)\in R$.
L87: A notion in nominal sets we will be making extensive use of is that of an orbit.
L88: ###### Definition 2.
L89: 
L90: Let $𝒳$ be a nominal set. Two elements $x,y\in 𝒳$ are nominally equivalent (denoted $x{\sim }_{\mathrm{𝗇𝗈𝗆}}y$) if $\pi \cdot x=y$ for some $\pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}$. Note ${\sim }_{\mathrm{𝗇𝗈𝗆}}$ is an equivalence relation.
L91: For each $x\in 𝒳$, we define its orbit $𝕆(x)$ to be its ${\sim }_{\mathrm{𝗇𝗈𝗆}}$-equivalence class; whereas for each finite $N\subseteq 𝔸$ we let ${𝕆}_{N}(x)$ be its $N$-orbit, i.e. its closure under permutations fixing $N$:
L92:  | $𝕆(x)$  | $=\{\pi \cdot x\mid \pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}\}$  | ${𝕆}_{N}(x)$  | $=\{\pi \cdot x\mid \forall a\in N.\pi (a)=a\}$  |
L93: 
L94: Observe that $𝕆(x)={𝕆}_{\mathrm{\varnothing }}(x)$. Moreover, for any $S\subseteq 𝒳$ with finite support we let:
L95: 
L96:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L97: 
L98: the closure of $S$ be $𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(S)=\{\pi \cdot x\mid x\in S\wedge \pi \in \mathrm{𝖯𝖾𝗋𝗆}\}$;
L99: 
L100:   * $\mathrm{■}$
L101: 
L102: the set of orbits of $S$ be $𝒪(S)=\{{𝕆}_{\mathrm{supp}(S)}(x)\mid x\in S\}$.
L103: We say that a nominal set $𝒳$ is orbit-finite if $𝒪(𝒳)$ is finite. If $𝒳$ is orbit-finite, we let its register index be ${r}_{i}(𝒳)=\mathrm{max}\{|\mathrm{supp}(x)|\mid x\in 𝒳\}$.
L104: Note in particular that $𝕆(x)=𝒞\mathrm{\ell }(\{x\})$, for any $x\in 𝒳$, and $𝒪(𝒳)=\{𝕆(x)\mid x\in 𝒳\}$. Given $N\subseteq {N}^{\prime }$ and any $x\in 𝒳$, we have ${𝕆}_{{N}^{\prime }}(x)\subseteq {𝕆}_{N}(x)\subseteq 𝒳$ and $\mathrm{supp}({𝕆}_{N}(x))\subseteq N$. Moreover, for any finitely supported $S\subseteq 𝒳$ we can see by inspection that:
L105:

L122: We next define nominal labelled transition systems, where states and labels form nominal sets, which retain a possibly unbounded history component but are otherwise orbit-finite. For that purpose, orbit-finiteness is relaxed to accommodate histories of unbounded size. One part of our solution is to use configurations comprising pairs of a state $s$ and a history $H$, with $\mathrm{supp}(s)\subseteq H$, where only the set of states is orbit-finite.
